title: Describing things
job: Size, colour, quality — agreement at length
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: AGREEMENT AT LENGTH is a grid, not a new idea. An adjective matches its noun in gender, number AND case, so M2's vysókiy turns up here as vysókuyu, vysókom and vysókikh. The honest framing: this is bookkeeping. The endings are few, they repeat across every adjective in the language, and the whole paradigm lives in one row's forms so it can be met as one thing rather than as a hundred.

THE GENITIVE OF ABSENCE, and it is the best sentence type in the module: net plus the genitive says the thing IS NOT HERE, and the sentence has no subject at all. Zdes' net magazína, U menyá net vrémeni. English cannot mirror it — "there is no shop" keeps a dummy there — and it is M1's subjectless shape again. net is L1-M2's word for "no", doing a second job rather than being a second word.

A WORD OF AMOUNT IS FOLLOWED BY THE GENITIVE. mnógo vodý, nemnógo sákhara, stakán vodý, cháshka cháya. That one line also explains two things already learnt without explanation: L1-M8's pyat' rubléy and L1-M4's pyat' chasóv were genitive plurals all along, because a number above four is a word of amount too.

FOUR OF THIS MODULE'S COLOURS CARRY A YÓ — zelyónyy, chyórnyy, zhyóltyy, deshyóvyy — and they must be written with it every time. The rule is not about telling words apart; it is about one word having one spelling, and colours are simply where it lands hardest in this course.

Half the grid costs nothing: for an inanimate masculine noun the accusative is identical to the nominative, so Ya khochú nóvyy stol needs no new shape at all. It is the feminine that moves visibly — knígu, krásnuyu — which is why every accusative sentence here is built on a feminine noun.

words.note: The whole paradigm this level shows, in one row: four nominative cells plus the feminine accusative. Old Russian for "beautiful" — Krásnaya plóshchad' is the Beautiful Square, not the red one.

sentences.trap: The ending is chosen by kníga and by nothing else. A speaker who knows the word for red still has to know the gender of the thing being described before they can say it.
sentences.sound: EH-ta KRAS-na-ya KNI-ga. The unstressed a's are all reduced, so the word runs shorter than it looks.

variations.changed: a masculine noun, so the masculine ending
a different colour, the same cell

variations.cue: This is a big red book
variations.changed: two adjectives, both agreeing with the same noun

mistake.why: kníga is feminine: Éhto krásnaya kníga.

sentences.usage: Pointing at something and naming it — the shape every description starts from.
sentences.mnemonic: The noun chooses the ending. Always.

words.note: A soft adjective, so its endings differ from krásnyy's throughout. Russian splits blue in two: síniy is the dark one and golubóy the light one, and neither covers the other.
A hard adjective like krásnyy, and stressed on the stem, so the mark never moves.

sentences.trap: BOTH words move: knígu is the accusative of kníga, and krásnuyu is the accusative to match it. The adjective does not sit still while the noun changes.
sentences.sound: ya kha-CHU KRAS-nu-yu KNI-gu. The two -u endings rhyme, which is the audible signal that the pair agree.

variations.changed: a soft adjective, so a different accusative ending
quality rather than colour
an inanimate masculine — the accusative costs nothing

mistake.why: Both words take the accusative: Ya khochú krásnuyu knígu.

sentences.usage: In a shop, pointing at one of two.
sentences.mnemonic: If the noun moves, the adjective moves with it.

words.note: Stem-stressed and entirely regular — the adjective to hold the pattern by when a harder one confuses it.
The yó is written in every shape and carries the stress, as a yó always does. Writing it with e would point the reader at the wrong syllable.

sentences.trap: magazín is masculine, so nóvyy takes -yy. The word looks like it ends in a doubled letter and does not — the first y is the vowel and the second the glide, exactly as in L1-M10's dóbryy.
sentences.sound: EH-ta NO-vyy ma-ga-ZIN. Both o's of magazín reduce, so only the last syllable is fully sounded.

variations.changed: a colour with a yó in it
feminine
neuter — the third cell of the same row

mistake.why: magazín is masculine: Éhto nóvyy magazín.

sentences.usage: Remarking on something that has just appeared in the street.
sentences.mnemonic: A yó is always stressed and always written.

sentences.cue: The green cup is on the table

words.note: Another yó word, and the first e reduces almost to i in speech: zi-LYO-nyy. The spelling keeps the e; the mouth does not.
The third yó colour. After zh the yó is written ё but sounds simply o, because zh cannot be softened — the letter records the history, not the sound.

sentences.trap: stolé is L1-M7's prepositional and has not changed. What is new is that the adjective in front of the SUBJECT agrees with the subject, and the case at the end of the sentence has nothing to do with it.
sentences.sound: zi-LYO-na-ya CHASH-ka na sta-LYE. The last word takes the stress of the phrase, which is why na leans onto it.

variations.cue: The yellow cup is on the table
variations.changed: a different colour, the same cell

variations.cue: The black cup is on the table
variations.changed: a third yó colour
masculine, and a different way of saying where

mistake.why: cháshka is feminine: Zelyónaya cháshka na stolé.

sentences.usage: Saying which one, when there is more than one.
sentences.mnemonic: Three of the six colours here carry a yó.

sentences.cue: This is a very expensive ticket

words.note: End-stressed, so the mark stays on the ending in every shape. It also means "dear" of a person, which is how letters open: Dorogóy Iván.
The fourth yó word of the module. Unlike English "cheap", it carries no insult — of a person it is simply not said.

sentences.trap: dorogóy pairs with L1-M8's stóit, and the two answer different questions: skól'ko stóit asks the price, dorogóy gives a verdict on it.
sentences.sound: EH-ta O-chin' da-ra-GOY bi-LYET. Two unstressed o's in dorogóy both reduce to a, so only the ending is heard clearly.

variations.cue: This is a very cheap ticket
variations.changed: the opposite verdict
feminine, and the stress stays on the ending
the adjective after the missing "is" rather than in front of the noun

mistake.why: The stress is on the ending: dorogóy.

sentences.usage: Complaining about a price, or explaining why you did not buy something.
sentences.mnemonic: Where the stress starts, it stays.

sentences.cue: This is a small clean room

words.note: The soft sign in the middle is heard: the l is palatalized. It is the ordinary word for small and carries no diminutive warmth by itself.
Clean of a room, pure of water or a language. Chístyy rússkiy means Russian without foreign words in it.
M1 opened only the neuter cell, inside bol'shóye spasíbo. Here is the paradigm it belongs to, end-stressed throughout.

sentences.trap: Two adjectives in a row and no comma between them. Russian stacks them exactly as English does, and both agree separately with the same noun.
sentences.sound: MA-lin'-ka-ya CHIS-ta-ya KOM-na-ta. Three words, three stresses, all on the first syllable — unusual, and it makes the line easy to say.

variations.cue: This is a big clean room
variations.changed: the opposite size
the adjective after the missing "is"
masculine

mistake.why: Both adjectives agree with kómnata: málen'kaya chístaya kómnata.

sentences.usage: Describing a room to someone who has not seen it.
sentences.mnemonic: Two adjectives, two endings, one noun choosing both.

words.note: L1-M4's magazín in the genitive. The thing that is absent goes into this case — which is the one place Russian marks a noun for not existing.
Neuter, and one of a small closed set that grow an -en- before every ending: vrémeni, not vrémya. U menyá net vrémeni is the commonest excuse in the language.

sentences.trap: There is no subject in this sentence and nothing is missing. English needs a dummy there; Russian puts the absent thing in the genitive and stops.
sentences.sound: zdyes' nyet ma-ga-ZI-na. net is emphatic and takes a beat of its own, which is what makes the sentence sound flat rather than apologetic.

variations.changed: a different absent thing
the same frame with a person in it — the negative of u menyá yest'
a different absent thing

mistake.why: What is absent goes in the genitive: Zdes' net magazína.

sentences.usage: Answering "is there a…?" — and it is a complete answer on its own.
sentences.mnemonic: Absent things go into the genitive.

sentences.cue: Give me a glass of water

words.note: A drinking glass, not the material and not spectacles. Russian has separate words for all three.
L1-M3's vodá in the genitive, which is what a word of amount demands. Note the stress: vódu (accusative) and vodý (genitive) differ only in where it falls.

sentences.trap: stakán vodý is "a glass OF water" with no word for "of". The genitive ending is the of, which is why it can never be dropped.
sentences.sound: DAY-tye mnye sta-KAN va-DY. The stress moves to the end in vodý, and the o reduces to a in front of it.

the same case, doing absence rather than amount

variations.cue: Give me a lot of water

mistake.why: A container takes the genitive: Dáyte mne stakán vodý.

sentences.usage: At a table, at a counter, at a kiosk.
sentences.mnemonic: The genitive ending IS the word "of".

words.note: L1-M1's chay in the genitive. Its own row rather than an edit to L1's, because an L1 file is never changed — the note points back instead.
L1-M3's sákhar in the genitive, and stem-stressed, so nothing moves but the ending.

sentences.trap: This is a complete order with no verb in it. Russian counters run on noun phrases, and adding a verb makes the request longer without making it politer.
sentences.sound: CHASH-ka CHA-ya pa-ZHA-lsta. The two ch words chime, which is why the phrase is easy to remember and easy to hear.

variations.changed: a word of amount instead of a container
kófe never changes shape, whatever the case
a different container and a different drink

mistake.why: A container takes the genitive: Cháshka cháya, pozháluysta.

sentences.usage: The commonest order in the country, said exactly like this.
sentences.mnemonic: kófe is the one that never moves.

sentences.cue: There is a lot of bread here

words.note: L1-M6's khleb in the genitive. The bare word is one syllable and unmarked; the moment an ending is added the stress becomes markable, and the mark appears.

sentences.trap: mnógo has been in the course since L1-M6 and has always demanded this case. What is new is not the word but the ending after it — and the same demand explains pyat' rubléy and pyat' chasóv, said for two levels without a reason.
sentences.sound: zdyes' MNO-ga KHLYE-ba. The kh is the sound at the end of Scottish "loch".
